title: What is known about 1RB0RB_1LC1RE_1LF0LD_1RA1LD_1RC1RB_---1LC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RB_1LC1RE_1LF0LD_1RA1LD_1RC1RB_---1LC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and reduced in Lean to a Collatz-like map. Sampled with the head in D at the left end, the tape is a run of ones with one hole: p ones, the hole, r ones. Lean proves, for all p, r ≥ 1, that one sample leads to the next by an explicit map f (the hole's position roughly halved when it is odd, a jump of the hole to the right end when it is even) in an explicit number of steps, or halts (p = 1), and that the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of (2, 2) under f reaches p = 1. Following the proved map, the kernel shows no halt in the first 103669 steps. Whether the orbit ever reaches p = 1 is a Collatz-like question; heuristically the chance is a few in 104.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: Hole at position 1 halts
claims.text: From D> 1 0 R with blank tape to the left, the machine reaches F on a 0 in 7 steps and halts, for every tape R.

claims.title: The hole map, for all p and r
claims.text: Write S(p, r) for the head in state D on the leftmost cell of 1^p 0 1^r, blank tape around. For all p, r ≥ 1: S(1, r) halts; S(3, r) → S(r+5, 2) for r odd and S(r+5, 1) for r even; S(2k+2, r) → S(3k+r+4, 1); S(2m+1, r) → S(m−1, m+r+3) for m ≥ 2, each in an exact number of steps cost p r (quadratic in k or m). Built from 12 symbolic rules found and proved by bbtools.symtm, chained by induction over the drift of a block across the ones, its consumption 11 by 11 at the right end, and the halving rounds.

claims.title: The reduction
claims.text: From blank tape the machine reaches S(2, 2) in 11 steps, and it halts if and only if the orbit of (2, 2) under the map reaches p = 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>3669</sup> steps
claims.text: The kernel follows the proved map for 30,000 samples from S(2, 2) (the numbers reach 1,835 digits) and adds up the proved step counts: more than 10<sup>3669</sup> steps, none of them a halt.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 21,646 cells have been visited and 21,644 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.07). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.471).

claims.title: The hole map, checked
claims.text: From each sample (D on the leftmost cell, reading 1; N cells, a single 0 at position p): p even: N' = N + p/2 + 2, p' = N' − 2; p odd, p ≥ 5: N' = N + 1, p' = (p−3)/2; p = 3: N' = N + 4, p' = N' − 3 (N odd) or N' = N + 3, p' = N' − 2 (N even); p = 1: halt. The machine follows this from every sample with N < 120 and 1 ≤ p ≤ N−2 (exhaustive), along the first 3·10<sup>7</sup> steps (31 samples) and at all 52 samples of the run to 2.9·10<sup>9</sup> steps. (Now proved for all N: see above; the check also confirms the step counts.)

claims.title: No halt in 10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: tools/c/tmrun.c: 1010 steps from blank tape without a halt (59,677 ones). The map from the run's first sample (N, p) = (5, 2), iterated 30,000 times (N then has 1,835 digits), never reaches p = 1 or 3.

claims.title: No closed tape language from windows up to 7
claims.text: bbtools.ctl with K = 2 to 7 closes but allows a halt (3 abstract halting configurations at every K); n-gram CPS (widths 3 to 7, -H, -U) fails, as it must: the halting configuration above is real.

claims.title: Why it probably never halts
claims.text: A halving chain p → (p−3)/2 → … ends at 1 only if it starts at p = 2<sup>j</sup> − 3; chains start at N − 2 (or N − 3 after p = 3), with N growing by a factor about 3/2 per even step. So the run must land exactly on a length like 2<sup>j</sup> − 1. Treating N as random at its scale, the expected number of hits beyond N ≈ 3·10<sup>4</sup> is about Σ<sub>j≥15</sub> 2/(2<sup>j</sup> ln 1.5) ≈ 3·10<sup>-4</sup>. The community lists the machine as Space Needle-like, probviously non-halting (bbchallenge wiki).

claims.title: Does it halt?
claims.text: Not proved either way. By the kernel claims above, the question is exactly whether the orbit of (2, 2) under the hole map ever reaches p = 1 (a halving chain p → (p−3)/2 → … starting at 2<sup>j</sup> − 3), a Collatz-like question with no visible invariant that rules it out.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but the question is now a clean number puzzle. Lean proves that this Turing machine halts exactly when a simple Collatz-like halving map, started from (2, 2), reaches p = 1, and that it does not halt in its first 10<sup>3669</sup> steps. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and explains the map.

facts.text: No halt, proved in Lean by following the proved map.
The reduction, proved in Lean for all values.
Heuristic chance that it ever halts.

sections.heading: Ones with a single hole
html: Every time the head is back at the left end in state D (reading a 1), the tape is N ones with exactly one 0, the hole, at position p. At step 1,137,813,213 for example:

Between two samples the head sweeps back and forth, either moving the hole left or extending the tape to the right by a cell every pair of sweeps (the square-root side). Each sample adds a cell at the left end, and samples get rarer as N grows: the logarithmic side.

sections.eyebrow: The rule from one sample to the next
sections.heading: Halve, or grow by a half
html:
• p odd, p ≥ 5: the hole jumps to (p − 3)/2 and N grows by 1;
  • p even: the tape grows to N' = N + p/2 + 2 and the hole ends at N' − 2;
  • p = 3: the tape grows by 3 or 4 and the hole goes near the right end;
  • p = 1: the machine halts.

Worked example from the run: (24,351, 24,349) → (24,352, 12,173) → (24,353, 6,085) → (24,354, 3,041) → (24,355, 1,519) → (24,356, 758), and 758 is even, so N' = 24,356 + 379 + 2 = 24,737 with the hole at 24,735, exactly as the machine does at step 1,569,459,635. A long halving chain like this one is the dangerous moment: it ended at 758, not at 1.

Proved for every N. For p = 2k+2 the head builds a block 0 1 D> 1 (11)^k 0 near the left end; each pass of 4k + 7 steps moves the whole block one cell right, past a 1; at the right end the block is eaten one 11 at a time, each bite leaving three 1s behind. For odd p = 2m+1 the head instead runs m halving rounds, each turning an 11 into one 1 left of the hole and one 1 right of it, which is what halves the hole's position. Each pass is a rule found and proved automatically by bbtools.symtm; Lean chains the passes by induction and adds up the exact step counts (lean/Map.lean, theorem sample_step).

sections.heading: Only through 2<sup>j</sup> − 1
html: Lean proves that a sample with the hole at position 1 halts 8 steps later, whatever the rest of the tape. A halving chain p → (p − 3)/2 reaches 1 only from 5, 13, 29, 61, …, 2j − 3, and chains start just left of the right end, at N − 2. So the run halts exactly if the tape length at some end-of-tape sample is 2j − 1.

The lengths grow by about a factor 3/2 per even step. Lean proves that the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the map, started from the first sample (p, r) = (2, 2) (the tape D> 1 1 0 1 1 at step 11), ever reaches p = 1 (halts_iff). Following the proved map for 30,000 samples (numbers of 1,835 digits), Lean's kernel adds up the proved step counts: no halt in the first 103669 steps (no_halt_10_3669). Treating the lengths as random at their scale, the chance of a hit from here on is about 3·10-4: probably non-halting, as the community thinks, but not proved.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.07). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.471).
After 109 steps the tape spans 21,646 cells (40 left of the start, 17,759 right), with a density of 1s of 1.0.

summary: Ones with a single hole (Space Needle-like): each time the head is back at the left end the hole jumps to (p-3)/2 if its position p is odd, else the tape grows by p/2 + 2; it halts exactly when a run of such halvings reaches position 1, i.e. when a tape length of the form 2^j - 1 turns up.
